stdout_tail:
Done. `analysis.py` and `result.json` are written.

## Finding

**Model performance** (held-out 25% test set, 48,790 rows after dropping 52 exact duplicates):
- HistGradientBoosting: ROC-AUC **0.9262**, PR-AUC 0.824, accuracy 0.872 (5-fold CV on train: 0.9281 ± 0.0013)
- Logistic regression: ROC-AUC 0.9048

**Permutation importance (GB, drop in test ROC-AUC, 20 repeats):**

| feature | drop | | feature | drop |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| capital-gain | **0.0578** | | hours-per-week | 0.0118 |
| age | 0.0462 | | education-num | 0.0030 |
| marital-status | 0.0425 | | workclass | 0.0027 |
| occupation | 0.0156 | | native-country / sex | ~0.0015 |
| capital-loss | 0.0142 | | fnlwgt | 0.0007 |
| relationship | 0.0141 | | race | 0.0005 |
| education | 0.0129 | | | |

**The single-feature ranking is misleading, and that's the substantive result.** This dataset contains two near-duplicate pairs: `education`/`education-num` (the same variable, categorical and ordinal) and `marital-status`/`relationship`. Permuting one member alone lets the model recover through its twin, so credit gets split. Permuting each block jointly (shared permutation index, preserving within-block joint structure) reorders things:

| block | AUC drop |
|---|---|
| **marital-status + relationship** | **0.1090** |
| capital-gain + capital-loss | 0.0744 |
| age | 0.0456 |
| education + education-num | 0.0255 |
| occupation | 0.0157 |
| hours-per-week | 0.0118 |
| workclass, sex, native-country, fnlwgt, race | ≤0.0026 |

So the honest answer is: **marital/family status is the largest single block of signal**, followed by the capital-gain/loss pair, age, education, occupation, and hours-per-week. Those six blocks carry essentially everything; `race`, `native-country`, `workclass`, `sex` and `fnlwgt` are near-zero.

**Cross-checks.** Logistic regression ranks `marital-status` first (0.126) and agrees on the tail (Spearman ρ = 0.71 vs GB), so the top group isn't a tree artifact. Leave-one-feature-out retraining shows tiny drops for `marital-status` (0.0003) and `education-num` (0.00005) — exactly the redundancy signature, since the retrained model routes around them via the twin column. `capital-gain` is the one feature that survives every method, including LOO (0.024), because nothing else in the data substitutes for it.

Two caveats worth flagging: `fnlwgt` is a census sampling weight, not a person-level attribute — its non-zero mutual information (0.039) is a kNN-estimator artifact on a continuous variable, and both permutation and LOO correctly put it at zero. And `sex` scoring near zero here means only that it adds little *given* marital-status/relationship/occupation, which are themselves strongly sex-patterned — it is not evidence of an absence of sex-related structure in the data.

One process note: my first run stalled because `permutation_importance(n_jobs=-1)` oversubscribed against HistGB's OpenMP threads on this machine. I killed it and reran single-process; the numbers above come from a complete, exit-0 foreground run.

parsed_result.summary: Marital/family status, education, capital-gain, age, occupation and hours-per-week carry essentially all the signal. On a held-out test set, permuting the single most important feature, capital-gain, costs 0.0578 ROC-AUC (baseline 0.9262) for a gradient-boosted model; permuting marital-status and relationship together -- they encode nearly the same thing and split credit when permuted alone -- costs 0.1090, the largest effect of any feature block. race, native-country, workclass and the survey weight fnlwgt are near-zero and fnlwgt is non-predictive by construction.
parsed_result.primary_metric_name: top feature permutation importance (drop in test ROC-AUC, gradient boosting, 20 repeats)
parsed_result.direction: capital-gain most important; marital/relationship block largest overall
parsed_result.methodological_choices: Model: HistGradientBoostingClassifier (max_iter=300, lr=0.1, 31 leaves, early stopping on a 15% internal split), categoricals ordinal-encoded and declared categorical, NaNs handled natively; compared against L2 logistic regression (C=1) with one-hot encoding (min_frequency=10, missing as its own level) and standardized numerics. Validation: single stratified 75/25 train/test split (seed 0), 52 exact duplicate rows removed first; all importances computed on the held-out test set, no hyperparameter tuning. Metric: ROC-AUC (class imbalance 24% positive left unweighted -- no class_weight or resampling -- since ROC-AUC is threshold- and prevalence-independent). Importance: permutation importance (20 repeats) as the primary method, cross-checked with leave-one-feature-out retraining, grouped permutation for correlated blocks (education+education-num, marital-status+relationship, capital-gain+capital-loss permuted with a shared index to preserve joint structure), and univariate mutual information; features ranked by mean rank across the four. Both education and education-num were kept despite being redundant, with the redundancy addressed by the grouped analysis rather than by dropping a column. Another researcher might use SHAP or impurity-based gains instead of permutation, drop the redundant/duplicated columns up front, use repeated CV rather than one split, optimize accuracy or PR-AUC, or tune hyperparameters.
